explanation: The unit mainly responds to frontal faces of furry mammals: eyes, a central nose or muzzle, and surrounding fur (foxes, cats, red pandas, hamster, meerkat, ferret, dog). It also fires on at least one face-like non-animal: a car's front, where the headlights and grille resemble eyes and a mouth.

The unit mainly responds to frontal faces of furry mammals, especially cats, foxes, red pandas and similar small carnivores, centered on the eyes-nose-muzzle arrangement. It also responds weakly to face-like frontal patterns, such as a car's front end.

The unit responds mainly to front-facing faces of small-to-medium furry mammals, especially cats, foxes and red pandas, centered on the eyes-nose-muzzle arrangement. It also responds to a face-like car front, likely because headlights and grille resemble eyes and muzzle.

The unit responds mainly to the faces of small furry mammals, with cats and foxes strongest (pointed ears, whiskered snouts, fur texture). It extends more weakly to related furry animals such as red pandas, hamsters, meerkats, ferrets, a lynx and a sheltie.

The unit responds mainly to the faces of small furry mammals, especially cats and foxes, and responds somewhat less to related animals such as red pandas, lynxes, hamsters, ferrets, meerkats and a sheltie.

The unit mainly responds to the faces of small, furry mammals seen from the front (cats, foxes, red pandas, and also a hamster, meerkat, ferret, and dog). It also fires on a red vintage convertible car, which has no meaningful connection to the animal theme.

The unit responds to faces of small furry mammals with pointed or upright ears and fluffy fur, mainly cats and foxes, and more weakly to similar animals such as red pandas, hamsters, meerkats, ferrets and a fluffy sheltie.

The unit responds to the faces and bodies of small, furry, cat- or fox-like mammals, most strongly to foxes and domestic cats. It responds more weakly to related fluffy small mammals such as red pandas, lynx, a hamster, a meerkat and a ferret.

The unit responds to the faces of small furry mammals with pointed or upright ears and fluffy fur, mostly cats, foxes and red pandas. It extends more weakly to related small fuzzy mammals such as a hamster, meerkat, ferret, lynx and a sheltie dog.

The unit fires on clause-boundary punctuation (commas, periods, semicolons) but mainly in documents about ships, boats and maritime topics, so it acts like a document-level 'nautical context' signal carried on punctuation. It also fires more weakly where the link is only through a word: 'anchor' (an electronics store, SEO anchor text) and 'vessels' in a medical report.
Fires on clause- and sentence-boundary punctuation (commas, periods, semicolons) in running prose. It is strongest when the document is about ships, boats or other maritime topics.

The unit fires on clause- and sentence-boundary punctuation (commas, periods, semicolons) and is strongest when the document is about boats, ships or other maritime topics. It fires more weakly on the same punctuation in unrelated prose.
The unit fires on commas and sentence-final periods, which are the punctuation marks that separate clauses, list items and sentences in running prose.

The unit fires on punctuation that marks clause or sentence boundaries, mainly commas and periods in running prose. It is strongest on commas that end an introductory phrase or a list item, or that come just before a contrasting or continuing clause.

The unit fires on the last token of a line, just before a line break, whatever that token is (a value, a brace, a word or punctuation).
The unit fires on the last token of a line, the token just before a newline, and it fires most strongly in structured or code-like text.

The unit mainly responds to the faces of small furry animals with pale or reddish fur, such as foxes, cats, red pandas, hamsters and ferrets, peaking around the muzzle and nose. It also responds separately to cars, especially sedans, station wagons and taxis.

The unit fires on clause- and sentence-boundary punctuation (commas, periods, semicolons) in documents whose earlier context contains ship or boat vocabulary such as ship, boat, vessel, anchor, crew or sailing. It acts like a nautical-context flag that is read out at punctuation, not on the nautical words themselves.

The unit fires on clause- and list-boundary punctuation (commas, periods, semicolons) in running prose. It fires most strongly when the document has a ship/boat/maritime theme (even a loose one such as the word 'anchor'), and more weakly on the same punctuation in documents with no such theme.

The unit fires on punctuation tokens, mainly commas and periods, that end a clause, sentence or list item in ordinary running prose. It is strongest in dense, declarative expository or narrative text such as marketing copy, news, policy text and complaints.

Fires on punctuation tokens, mainly commas and sentence-final periods, that mark clause, list or sentence boundaries in running prose. It is strongest on commas inside lists or before a following clause, and weaker in plain expository or catalog-style text.

The unit fires on punctuation tokens, mainly commas and sentence-final periods (including abbreviation periods such as "Capt."), that mark clause, list-item or sentence boundaries in ordinary running prose.

The unit fires on the last token of a line, the token immediately before a newline, whatever that token is (punctuation, word, number, brace). It is strongest in code, config and license headers, and somewhat weaker at line ends in prose, lists and headings.

The unit fires on the last token of a line, the token right before a newline, whatever that token is. It fires hardest in structured or code-like text (config files, license headers, code signatures, CSS, doc comments) and moderately on line-final tokens in lists, headings and prose paragraph ends.

The unit fires on the last token of a line, the token right before a newline, whatever that token is. It fires most strongly in code, config files and structured or formatted text, and more weakly at the ends of prose lines or paragraphs.

The unit fires most strongly on the word 'cheese' and on cheese names (cheese/cheeses, Mozzarella, Brie, cottage/cream cheese), and it fires at mid strength on C/C++ preprocessor directives, both the '#' and the 'define'/'include' token. Brie fires even when it is used as a person's name (Alison Brie).

The unit fires most strongly on the word "cheese" or a cheese name (cheese, cheeses, Mozzarella, Brie), including when "Brie" is a person's name. It fires moderately on C/C++ preprocessor directives, on both the '#' and the 'define'/'include' token.

The unit fires most strongly on words for cheese, both the word 'cheese/cheeses' and cheese names such as Mozzarella and Brie, including the Brie token when it is used as a person's name. Separately, it fires at about 60% strength on C/C++ preprocessor directives, on both the '#' token and the 'define'/'include' token.

The unit fires on the word 'coffee' and on coffee drinks and coffee-related terms such as latte, barista, the 'm' of mocha/macchiato and coffeehouse, with the token for coffee itself firing strongest. It responds more weakly to café/cafe/cafes and only faintly (about 4) to 'Java', most likely through Java's association with coffee.

Fires on the word 'coffee' and coffee drinks (latte, mocha, barista), with moderate activation on café/coffeehouse words. Weaker activation appears on 'Java' as a programming language, probably through Java's association with coffee.

The unit fires on words for coffee and coffee drinks: 'coffee'/'Coffee' and 'latte' reach the top of the range, with 'barista' and the start of 'mocha' also high. It responds more weakly to café/coffeehouse words ('Cafe', 'Café', 'cafes', 'Coffeehouse'), and weakest of all to 'Java' used as the name of the programming language.

The unit fires on the token just before a period that sits inside a token string rather than ending a sentence: decimals (-0.07, 29.9), domain names (www., github.com), code member access (target.nodeName, params.delete), abbreviations and initials (N.C., U.S., i.e., A. actinomycetemcomitans), and run-together text ('recognized.The'). Ordinary sentence-final periods ('have.', 'gaming.') give weaker activation.

The unit fires on the token that comes directly before a period '.', most strongly when that period is internal rather than sentence-final: decimal points (0.07, 29.9), domain or file-name dots (www., github.com), code member-access dots (e.target, local_params.delete) and abbreviation dots (N.C., R. 47.5, U.S., i.e.). Tokens before ordinary sentence-ending periods activate more weakly, though still noticeably.

The unit fires on the token immediately before a period '.', and fires hardest when that period is internal to a larger token sequence rather than ending a sentence. Typical strong cases are decimal points (0.07, 29.9), URL or domain dots (www., github.com), code member access (target.nodeName, params.delete) and abbreviation dots (N.C., U.S., R. 47.5).

The strongest trigger is the tokens of a bird name (swan, owl, finch, kestrel, duck, sparrow, falcon, flamingo, heron), whether the word refers to the bird or is reused as a surname, title, idiom or acronym. A separate, weaker trigger (about 5-7) is abbreviated month names in dates, such as Sep, Oct., Nov., Aug., Feb., Sept.

The unit fires most strongly on tokens that spell a bird name, whether the word means the bird or not: surnames (Finch, Swan, Heron, Falcon), idioms (lame duck, green swan), titles (Swan Lake), band names (Flamingos), function names (Kestrel) and acronyms (SWAN). Separately and more weakly (about 5-7), it fires on abbreviated month names written before a day number, such as "Oct. 13", "Aug. 10" and "23 Sep 16".

The unit fires most strongly on tokens that spell bird names (swan, owl, finch, kestrel, duck, sparrow, falcon, flamingo, heron), whatever the word means in context: surnames, acronyms, idioms, band names and code identifiers all count. Separately, it fires moderately on abbreviated month names in dates (Sep, Oct., Nov., Aug., Feb., Sept.).

Responds to the front-facing face of a small or medium furry mammal, especially cats, foxes, red pandas and similar animals with fur, two forward eyes, a snout and upright ears, likely reacting to a fur-textured face with an eyes-and-nose layout.

Fires on the faces of small furry mammals seen from the front: domestic cats, foxes, red pandas, hamsters, ferrets, meerkats, lynx. The strongest responses are to forward-facing furry heads with pointed ears and visible eyes.

The unit responds mainly to the faces of small furry mammals, typically seen from the front with eyes and ears visible: foxes, cats, red pandas, a hamster, a meerkat, a ferret, lynxes and a fluffy dog. One unexplained exception is a maroon vintage convertible at activation 9, which may be picking up the shared reddish-brown colour or a front 'face-like' grille and headlights.

The unit responds to frontal faces of small, furry, pointy-eared mammals: cats, foxes, red pandas and lynx most strongly, with hamsters, meerkats and ferrets as weaker related cases. Images built around other things push it negative, especially flat-faced or droopy-eared dogs (pugs, boxers, mastiffs), birds and hairless or smooth-skinned animals.

Responds to faces of small, furry, pointy-eared mammals such as cats, foxes, red pandas, lynx, ferrets and hamsters, with fluffy fur texture and alert upright ears. It is suppressed by flat-faced, short-haired dogs (pugs, mastiffs, boxers) and by birds.

Fires on the faces of small to medium furry mammals with pointed or upright ears and soft fur, such as foxes, cats, red pandas, lynx, hamsters, meerkats and ferrets, often looking toward the camera; weaker offshoots include fluffy dogs like a sheltie.

Fires on sentence and list punctuation (commas, periods, semicolons) in documents whose earlier context involves ships, boats or other nautical and maritime themes. It seems to carry a document-level 'ship/vessel/anchor' topic signal that it expresses on punctuation tokens rather than on the nautical words themselves.

The unit fires on clause and list punctuation (commas, periods, semicolons) in documents about ships, boats and other maritime vessels. It appears to carry a 'ship/vessel topic' signal at each sentence or list boundary, not on the topic words themselves.

The unit fires on clause- and sentence-ending punctuation (commas, periods, semicolons) in documents that have a ship, boat or nautical context, apparently carrying that topic forward at each boundary. It does not fire on the nautical words themselves.

The unit fires on clause- and sentence-boundary punctuation (commas and periods) in running prose. It responds most strongly to commas that close a clause or list item partway through a sentence, and somewhat less to sentence-final periods.
Fires on commas and periods in running prose, the clause and sentence boundary punctuation, and tends to stay active on most punctuation marks throughout a passage rather than on content words.

The unit fires on clause- and sentence-boundary punctuation (commas and periods) in running prose. It is strongest on commas that separate list items or clauses (e.g. 'personal customer service«,» and', 'Pakistan«,» but').

Fires on the last token of a line, the position just before a newline. It is strongest in structured or boilerplate text such as code, YAML/config, license headers, doc comments and method signatures, where a line break is highly predictable.

The unit fires on the last token of a line, the position just before a newline, regardless of what kind of token sits there (a value, brace, punctuation, word or name piece) or what kind of text it is.

Fires on the last token of a line, the position just before a line break. It is strongest in structured or boilerplate text such as code, config/YAML, license headers, method signatures and CSS selectors, and weaker at line ends in lists, headings and prose paragraphs.

The unit fires mainly on the word 'cheese' and on cheese names (cheese, cheeses, Mozzarella, Brie, cream/cottage cheese), and separately fires moderately on C/C++ preprocessor directive tokens ('#' plus 'include' or 'define').

The unit's main job is the word 'cheese' and cheese names (cheese, cheeses, Mozzarella, Brie), firing on the cheese token itself in food contexts. Separately, it fires at moderate strength on C/C++ preprocessor directives (the '#' and 'include'/'define' tokens).

The unit fires most strongly on the word 'cheese' and on cheese names (Mozzarella, Brie, 'cheeses'), including the surface token 'Brie' when it is the actress's name. Separately, it fires at mid strength on C/C++ preprocessor directives ('#' plus 'include'/'define').

Fires on the word 'coffee' and closely related coffee-drink tokens such as latte, barista and the 'm' starting a mocha/macchiato, peaking on 'coffee' itself in any context. It is weaker on café/coffeehouse words and weakest on 'Java', which links to coffee through the name.

Fires on the word 'coffee' and coffee-drink tokens such as latte, coffee house and barista, with weaker spread to café/cafe names and a faint response to 'Java' (the programming language, likely via the coffee sense of Java).

Fires on the word 'coffee' and closely related coffee-drink terms (latte, barista, mocha), with weaker activation on café/coffeehouse words and on 'Java' as a programming language, which is a coffee synonym.

The unit fires on the token just before a period, and fires most strongly when that period is internal rather than sentence-ending: decimal points (-0.07, 29.9), URL and domain dots (www., github.com), code member access (target.nodeName, params.delete), and abbreviations (N.C., U.S., i.e., R. 47.5). Tokens before an ordinary sentence-final period fire more weakly.

The unit fires on the token just before a period that is likely to be an internal, non-sentence-ending dot: a decimal point, a domain or URL dot, a code member access, an abbreviation, or a period with no following space. It peaks where the next character is '.' joined directly to more text.

Fires on the token just before a period that does not end a sentence, where the dot is followed directly by more characters: decimal points (-0.07, 29.9), domain and path dots (www.aace.co.uk, github.com), code member access (e.target.classList), and abbreviation dots (N.C., U.S., i.e., A.).

The unit fires mainly on bird-name tokens, even when the word is used as a surname, title or acronym (swan, owl, finch, kestrel, duck, sparrow, falcon, flamingo, heron). Separately, it fires moderately on abbreviated month names before a day number in dates (Sep, Oct., Nov., Aug., Feb., Sept.).

The unit fires mainly on bird names, whatever role they play: literal birds, surnames (Finch, Swan, Heron), product or band names (Kestrel, Flamingos), idioms (lame duck, green swan), and even acronyms that spell a bird (SWAN). A separate, weaker response fires on abbreviated month names in dates (Sep, Oct, Nov, Aug, Feb, Sept).

The unit fires most strongly on bird-name tokens, and it does so even when the word is a surname, band name, acronym or idiom (Swan, owls, Finch, Kestrel, lame duck, black/green swan, sparrow, Falcon, Flamingos, SWAN, Heron). A separate, weaker response sits on abbreviated month names that come right before a day number in dates (Sep, Oct., Nov., Aug., Feb., Sept.).

The unit mainly responds to the faces of small furry mammals: cats, foxes and red pandas most strongly, with weaker responses to a hamster, meerkat, ferret, dog and arctic fox. It also fires strongly on a vintage maroon convertible car, which has no clear connection to that concept.

The unit mainly responds to the faces of small-to-medium furry mammals, especially cats and foxes, with related extensions to red pandas, hamsters, meerkats, ferrets, lynx and a dog. It also fires strongly on an unrelated concept, a vintage red convertible car.
The unit mainly responds to the faces of small furry mammals, especially cats and foxes, and also fires on related animals such as red pandas, a hamster, a meerkat, a ferret, a lynx and a sheltie.

The unit responds to the faces of small furry carnivore-like mammals with pointed ears and whiskers, mainly cats and foxes, and more weakly to red pandas, hamsters, meerkats, ferrets and lynx. It is suppressed by dogs (especially flat-faced breeds like pugs and mastiffs), birds and non-furry objects.

The unit responds to faces of small furry mammals with pointed or upright ears, mainly foxes and cats (domestic cats, lynx, red pandas), and more weakly to related small mammals such as hamsters, meerkats, ferrets, and one fluffy sheltie.

The unit responds to faces of small furry mammals with pointed or upright ears, mainly cats and foxes, and less strongly to related animals such as red pandas, hamsters, a lynx, a meerkat, a ferret and a sheltie.

The unit fires most strongly on words that name cheese, such as 'cheese', 'cheeses', 'mozzarella' and 'Brie'. Separately and more weakly, it fires on the '#' and the 'define' or 'include' that begin preprocessor lines in C and C++ code.

The unit fires most strongly on the word 'cheese' and on names of cheeses (Mozzarella, cheeses, and even 'Brie' used as a person's name, Alison Brie). Separately, it fires at a moderate level on C/C++ preprocessor directives such as '#include' and '#define'.

The unit fires most strongly on the word for cheese, including specific kinds like mozzarella and Brie. Separately, it fires at moderate strength on C and C++ preprocessor lines such as #include and #define.

The unit fires on the center of a small furry mammal's face, the nose, muzzle and whisker area, and responds most to cats and foxes. It responds more weakly to similar faces of hamsters, red pandas, ferrets, meerkats and a sheltie.
The unit fires on the nose and muzzle of small furry mammals seen face-on, especially cats and foxes, and most strongly where pale or warm-coloured fur surrounds a small nose.

The unit fires on the middle of a small furry animal's face seen head-on, centered on the nose and muzzle, especially narrow, light or pinkish snouts with whiskers, as on cats, foxes, hamsters, ferrets and red pandas.

The unit fires most strongly on bird-name words (swan, owl, finch, kestrel, duck, sparrow, falcon, flamingo, heron). It fires on them even when they are surnames, idioms, band names or acronyms, and it responds more weakly to abbreviated month names before a day number (Sep, Oct, Nov, Aug, Feb, Sept).

The unit fires most strongly on bird names, whether they mean the bird or are used as proper names, surnames, acronyms or idioms (Swan Lake, owls, Finch, Kestrel, lame duck, green swan, sparrow, Falcon Scott, Flamingos, SWAN, Heron). It also fires moderately on abbreviated month names in dates (Sep, Oct., Nov., Aug., Feb., Sept.).

The unit fires most strongly on bird names, whether used literally or not, including surnames (Swan, Finch, Heron), product names (Kestrel), idioms (lame duck, green swan) and acronyms (SWS, SWAN). It also fires moderately on abbreviated month names that come before a date (Sep, Oct, Nov, Aug, Feb, Sept).

The unit responds most strongly to cat-like and fox-like small mammals (domestic cats, foxes, red pandas, hamsters, ferrets, meerkats), especially clear frontal views of the face. Separately, it responds moderately to cars and other road vehicles.

The unit mainly responds to frontal faces of small and medium furry mammals with pointed ears and visible eyes, such as cats, foxes, red pandas, hamsters, meerkats and ferrets. It also has a separate, moderate response to cars, especially convertibles and sports cars.

The unit responds most strongly to close-up, front-facing faces of cats and similar small furry mammals (foxes, red pandas, hamsters, meerkats, ferrets). It also responds moderately and consistently to cars, which share nothing meaningful with those animals.

The unit mainly responds to the faces of small furry mammals with pointed ears, eyes and whiskers, such as cats, foxes, red pandas, ferrets, hamsters and fluffy small dogs. It also has a separate, weaker response to convertible cars.

The unit fires most strongly on the faces of cat- and fox-like small mammals (foxes, domestic cats, red pandas, lynx, hamster, meerkat, ferret). Separately, it gives moderate-to-strong responses to cars of many kinds (convertibles, sports cars, sedans/wagons, vintage cars).

The unit responds most strongly to frontal faces of small furry mammals with pointed ears, such as foxes, cats, red pandas, hamsters, lynx, meerkats and ferrets. Separately, it also responds consistently to cars, especially convertibles and sports cars.
The unit fires on commas and periods in running prose, at clause, list-item and sentence boundaries. It is a punctuation or boundary detector rather than a detector of any particular topic.
The unit fires on punctuation that marks the end of a clause or sentence, mainly commas and periods, in running prose.

The unit fires on commas and periods that end clauses, list items, or sentences in running prose. Commas mid-sentence before a following clause are the strongest, sentence-final periods are close behind, and abbreviation and number-separator periods and commas fire more weakly.

The unit fires most strongly on bird names, including when they appear as surnames, product names or acronyms (swan, owls, finch, kestrel, duck, sparrow, falcon, flamingos, heron). It separately fires at moderate strength on abbreviated month names in dates (Sep, Oct., Nov., Aug., Feb., Sept.).

The unit fires most strongly on bird-name words (swan, owl, finch, kestrel, duck, sparrow, falcon, flamingo, heron), whether or not they refer to birds: surnames, band names, idioms, acronyms and code identifiers all count. It also fires moderately on abbreviated month names in dates (Sep, Oct, Nov, Aug, Feb, Sept).

The unit fires mainly on bird-name tokens (swan, owls, finch, kestrel, duck, sparrow, falcon, flamingos, heron), including when the word is used as a surname, band name, acronym or idiom. Separately, it fires moderately on abbreviated month names in dates (Sep, Oct, Nov, Aug, Feb, Sept).
